books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Daniel Webster, speech in the Senate, March 7, 1850

stimulus.source_note: Daniel Webster, speech in the Senate, March 7, 1850 (Congressional Globe, 31st Congress, 1st session, Appendix — Webster's revised text). Public domain.
stimulus.text:
Mr. President, — I wish to speak to-day, not as a Massachusetts man, nor as a Northern man, but as an American, and a member of the Senate of the United States.

. . .

I speak to-day for the preservation of the Union. “Hear me for my cause.” I speak to-day, out of a solicitous and anxious heart, for the restoration to the country of that quiet and that harmony which make the blessings of this Union so rich and so dear to us all.

. . .

Desirous of immediate connection with the United States, [California's] Senators were appointed and representatives chosen, . . . asking, in behalf of their State, that the state may be admitted into this Union as one of the United States. This constitution, Sir, contains an express prohibition against slavery, or involuntary servitude, in the State of California. . . . This prohibition against slavery, it is said, was inserted with entire unanimity.

rationales.A: Background from the books: Webster was a senator from Massachusetts, a free state, and he opens by refusing to speak “as a Massachusetts man, nor as a Northern man.”
rationales.B: Background from the books: Webster spoke on March 7, 1850, months before the compromise laws passed in September 1850; he was arguing for measures not yet law.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Webster was a Massachusetts Whig whose antislavery supporters denounced his support for the compromise, including its fugitive slave provisions; his “American” framing was a deliberate break with his section.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Henry Clay drafted the compromise resolutions, and Stephen A. Douglas later carried the separate bills; Webster supported the plan in debate but did not write or introduce it.
rationales.general:
1. Background from the books: Webster was a Massachusetts senator, speaking to a Northern audience that hated the compromise.
2. Background from the books: his Union-first framing cost him the trust of the antislavery voters who sent him there.
3. See the method: he renounces his section's labels first, so the Union plea sounds like an American speaking, not a section pleading.
Remember: always ask who a speaker risks angering; the answer tells you how much his words cost him.
